4 JACOB NOEL

Alongside these monodromy results, we isolate a separability consequence of the binomial Newton face and the Brylawski identity. Following [10], a polynomial F ∈Z[X, Y ] satisfying

(Y −1)rF  Y Y −1, Y  = Y r+s (1.3)

is a normalized (r + s, r)-Brylawski polynomial. For positive weights, in(s,r) F denotes the sum of the monomials on the corresponding maximal face of the Newton polygon.

Theorem 1.5 (Newton–Brylawski separability). Let r, s > 0 and let F ∈Z[X, Y ] be monic in X, satisfy (1.3), and have in(s,r) F = Xr + Y s. Put g = gcd(r, s), and let lbe an odd prime such that

l| r, l∤s, g < l. (1.4)

Then F mod lis separable in X over Fl(Y ). If, moreover, r and vl(r) are odd, then

discX F(X, Y ) /∈Q(Y )×2. (1.5)

The separability conclusion permits good specializations and their Frobenius factor patterns. The discriminant conclusion says that geometric monodromy contains an odd permutation, because the discriminant of a separable polynomial is a square precisely when its root action lies in the alternating group. Theorem 1.5 is independent of Theorem 1.1; it applies when the first root- dependent correction is unavailable.

1.1. Proof strategy. The trace arguments use the density bound to control the entire polar part of the roots at infinity: the branches share a common polar series multiplied by their roots-of-unity labels. Cancellation of those labels in a block sum therefore cancels every polar term. Classical constancy and integrality arguments then force an exact block-trace identity (Theorem 7.1). The defect bound thus converts a finite phase calculation into a divisibility constraint on the number of blocks; higher coefficients can exclude the remaining candidate trace identities. For the hypercube proof, set

g = gcd(N, E), L = N/g, h = σ/g.

The integer g is the number of inertia orbits above Y = ∞, each of length L. The proof separates into the cases g = 1 and g > 1; when N is prime, transitivity alone gives primitivity. Since N prime forces g = 1 (then n is prime and N ≡1 (mod n)), the three regimes are nested:

{N prime} transitivity ⊂ {g = 1} centered sums ⊂ {g ≥1} characteristic two

The labels name the ingredient that primitivity needs at each level beyond the previous one; the transposition of Section 4 is common to all three. When N is prime, that is, a Mersenne prime, a transitive group of prime degree is primitive, and Theorem 1.1 follows from irreducibility, the simple branch point, and Lemma 7.7. When g = 1 and N is composite, the centered block sums of Section 7.1 exclude every nontrivial block system; this is the argument of Theorem 1.3, and reduction modulo two is unnecessary. When g > 1, which first happens at n = 6, centered sums give the divisibility condition k | g, and the characteristic-two action of Sections 5 and 6 forces the number of blocks to be coprime to g. Table 2.2(a) records the parameters in small dimensions; Remark 7.6 works through the three block-system tests for n = 6.

At infinity we shift to the rank-generating polynomial and rescale by the density defect. Strict uniform density leaves the binomial initial face XN + Y σ, which gives the inertia cycles. Edge isoperimetry then shows that single edges are the unique nonempty nonspanning subsets contribut- ing to the first root-dependent correction. Its coefficient E has two uses: together with the prime supplied by Lemma 2.1, it produces a simple branch point; it also centers the sums attached to a hypothetical block system.
